title: State of the Art of Platform Engineering • Abby Bangser & Charles Humble • GOTO 2026

segments.text: Hello and welcome to this mini series
for GoTo called the state of the art.
This series will explore Gen AI fairly
obviously, but also other emerging
trends and things like new practices,
new programming languages and on this
particular episode, platform
engineering. I'm Charles Humble. I have
over 30 years of experience as a
programmer, architect and CTO and I'm
currently working mainly as a freelance
consultant and writer and podcaster. And
I'm joined today by Abby Bangser. Abby
is a principal engineer at Syntasso
delivering practices, which is an open
source cloud native framework for
building internal developer platforms on
Kubernetes.
Her keen interest in supporting internal
developer development comes from over a
decade of experience in consulting and
product delivery roles across platform,
site reliability and quality
engineering. I'm very much looking
forward to this conversation. I've been
doing a lot of writing and researching
around how Gen AI is impacting on the
various practices and processes of
software engineering. As a discipline,
we are in flux. No one knows what
software engineering will look like in
two years and we're facing some very
real challenges around how we do things
like validate code if LLMs generate most
of it. I think you can see some of this
playing out with how some of the
established IDE vendors, for example,
are struggling to adapt to this new
world. And in that context, I'm very
interested to hear Abby's perspective on
the role of platform engineering.
Um just because I think it's another of
those disciplines that will be impacted
by the changes that we're seeing. So
Abby, welcome to the show.
>> Thank you so much for having me. It's
quite the intro and I absolutely agree
that AI is affecting all disciplines and
platforms in particular, I think are are
coming into the forefront right now,
which is really exciting to see.
>> It is, yeah. So I really want to get
into that. Let's do a little bit of
background first. So I interviewed
Syntasso co-founder Paula Kennedy for
another podcast back in, I think it was
early 2023. And at the time, she sort of
suggested that platform engineering was,
you know, kind of finding its footing
still. So, I was curious, how would you
characterize where the discipline stands
today?
>> Yeah, I think it's
I think we're still a little bit finding
footing, but a lot more mature in some
areas. So, what I would say is that the
understanding that centralization of
offerings within an organization is
valuable is pretty well understood now,
right? So, we've been through a
transition from centralized ops to
devops and decentralization of that. And
platforms bring that re-centralized, but
bringing it the centralization with the
self-service, you know, unblocked value
stream experience, ideally. And I think
people are seeing the value of
centralizing for the the cost savings of
duplication across the org, the benefits
of of compliance and coherency of their
requirements in inside of the business.
But, I think that where, you know,
you're you're asking about platform
engineering and the practice of actually
building those platforms. And I think
the architecture patterns are still
getting solidified as we speak. What I
mean by that is that too many
organizations right now are
re- a little bit rehashing that
experience of centralized ops. They've
taken the the reasoning to move from
devops into platforms and seen the value
in it and gone to do it, but the
execution has gone back to kind of a
centralized team or group of teams that
has started to feel the pressure of
trying to keep up with an entire
organization, right? With that
centralized view. And so, the
architecture of engineering a
marketplace internally to try and enable
that scaling of building the platforms
is something that we are
seeing emerge. I saw, I think, three or
four different talks about this at
KubeCon in the autumn of 2025 in Atlanta
in the US and also it became sort of a
mainstream topic of conversation by the
time we got to EU in March of 2026. So,
we're there, but we're not seeing it as
widely spread as I I I'd like to or as
the industry needs it to be, I think.
>> Right, yes. And you you co-led the Sense
F platform working group then
contributed to the platform engineering
maturity model.
So, what does it actually mean to be
mature at platform engineering, would
you say?
>> We had the discussions. It's basically
being mature at software engineering in
a lot of ways, but I think the value of
that maturity model is it brings it into
the context of the domain of platforms,
which
a lot of people who are building
platforms today have not historically
built software. They've built
infrastructure, they've built
infrastructure as code, but building,
you know, Terraform and Puppet and Chef
and and all those great tools is not the
same thing as building a service. And
that ability to build something that can
evolve over time and can set strong APIs
with its
you know, fellow services both up and
downstream is something that I think
Gregor Hope has talked about as floating
platforms. Again, bringing the concepts
of software engineering but to the
platform domain, he talks about the need
for a platform to have stable offerings,
but the evolution of how they deliver
those offerings, the the actual
implementation needs to float above
things that become commodity in the
industry. And I think those are the
types of concepts that we tried to
bring to the platform domain with that
maturity model.
>> Right, yes. Yeah. You also co-wrote the
O'Reilly platform as a product report.
And I was So again, my conversation with
Paula, we were talking quite a lot about
this idea of of
treating a platform as a product versus,
you know, just sort of saying those
words and kind of wishful thinking. So,
I was curious as to, you know, what does
it look like when an organization is
genuinely treating platform as a
product?
>> I think
I look at just consuming other products
and I think about how much I wish people
would
uh focus on their value prop more when
I'm a user of a product. So, one of the
really quick tests of a platform is
where the team has said no to a feature
uh or where they have actually
deprecated something cuz it shows that
they have a clarity of what they offer
versus what you can do off platform or
outside of the scope of what they are
offering. That shows they have actual
product you kind of scope to it. So,
that's a really kind of cheap way uh to
identify if you're if you're really
thinking about this like a scoped
product or not, I think.
>> Right. Yes.
Yeah. There's another So, Daniel Bryant,
who I also know quite well cuz he and I
worked together at uh Improbable back in
the day. He's now also at Snyk so and
he's argued that developer portals and
CI/CD pipelines kind of creates a he
calls it a platform facade. Can you
unpack that a bit for me? What does he
mean by that?
>> Yeah, so
the way that I you know, I've had lots
of chats with him about this. I think
when you think about a platform, you
want to be able to get something that is
self-service. So, on demand, I get it
when I want it without having to worry
about vacation days for the the platform
team and so forth. Uh and I want it to
be compliant for my business. So, I
don't want to have to worry about
security coming after me and telling me
I have to do all sorts of things. And I
want it to be sort of working in the
future. I don't want to have to be
thinking about upkeep for it forever.
It's kind of as a service to a certain
extent and that's it's managed to a
certain extent.
And when we think about those kind of
expectations on something coming off the
platform,
you can build
a facade of that, what looks good to
that, with a portal, which is a a UI for
users, that can make requests for
things, right? They can send in a form
that says I'd like a service of some
sort, a a test environment of some sort,
with these characteristics, and send
that form off, and it appears quite
self-service because they get back a URL
for their test environment, or, you
know, whatever that the return
object is.
But, if the execution behind that portal
is a
it is a pipeline, those pipelines are
built for kind of one-off delivery of
something, one-off like changes. That's
what they're they're purpose-built for.
So, what happens when you need to update
this thing? Or, what happens if you
change something in and your delivered
service starts to drift from the
desired service? How are you going to
know, how are you going to identify the
drift, reconcile the drift? Um it is a
problem from the user's perspective.
Also from the user's perspective, if I
can only access this service through a
UI, what happens when I need to script
access to the service? What happens when
I want access when I want my AI agent to
work on my behalf and access the
service? Like,
it all of a sudden you're building a lot
of logic and expectation into a single
type of interface.
So, the combination of
a single interface that maybe shouldn't
own a lot of decisions and business
logic like a UI, and a back end that can
only really do one-off changes and
doesn't keep that longevity of
reconciliation, drift detection, as well
as makes it difficult to change every
instance that's been through that
pipeline. Try try updating all test
environments to patch a bug, uh or patch
a security risk.
Those kinds of things are are where
you're missing the nuance of the value
of a platform, where you're getting that
facade, it looks good, it feels good to
get started with it, but when you dig
under the surface a little bit, it
doesn't quite hold up. Um, so I think
that's
the way we try and explain that.
>> Right. Yes. Yeah, I'm with you. I've
also had you speak quite a bit about
platform decay as a kind of a challenge
for the field. So, how does decay happen
and what are maybe the early warning
signs that a platform team ought to be
looking out for?
>> Uh, the reason that the word decay
started getting used is because it did
mirror the physical world with decay.
So, this idea that, um, it's easier to
maintain things than it is to fix them.
And decay is something where you start
to notice that you need more maintenance
to be effective, uh, and you and you're
at risk of getting towards a point where
you just have to stop and fix things.
So, how do you know if you're sort of
allowing yourself to drift towards, uh,
you know, a stop moment for you? One of
the ways I think in tech that you can
know is if you start kind of cutting
corners to to make change. So, uh, a
really concrete example would be if you
find yourself attaching a change to the
to a place that it's not really suitable
within your code base, but it's just
easier to do that than to go about the
the right architecture because you have
some sort of friction there on doing it
the the quote unquote right way or the
way that you would prefer to do it. Um,
and so whenever you start finding
yourself, uh, operating because of
avoiding friction versus because it's
the the designed way you want to work,
that can be indicators that the design
you originally implemented, no matter
how great it was at the time, may not be
keeping up with what you need today.

need to invest in in patching and
maintaining that architecture so that it
can continue to support you rather than
having to hit a moment where you have a
a rebuild,
uh, you know, project that we all know
is really hard to to pull off at scale,
right?
>> Right, yeah. I kind of I'm picking that
a bit more cuz I think one of the
challenges
that we've all experienced in different
places in different ways in the industry
is
how you make the case for maintenance
work to your stakeholders, to your
business stakeholders, who quite often,

interested in funding new features than
they are in doing the maintenance work.
Do you have any kind of thoughts or
advice on that?
>> Uh so, I think it's something that we
get I end up speaking a lot about
because it's true for actually almost
all platform work often times. Even
though it's not maintenance work, it
feels sort of divorced from the revenue
of the business and therefore it can
feel like how do you make a case for
this thing when everyone wants to be
doing revenue generating changes. Um so,
it's quite just to be clear, it's quite
difficult. I think what you're trying to
do is keep track of the impact on costs
a lot of times uh and the impact on
opportunity costs is the best way to go
about it because that is
forward-thinking rather than becoming a
cost center.
So, on on the cost side of things, you
can keep track of the what that friction
is causing in your system. So, numbers
of tickets, uh
duration that infrastructure is living
for beyond when it should. So, I was
having a conversation just today with a
team that's saying the reason they're
getting funding to invest in their
platform is because they uh are finding
environments are living longer than they
should because the teams requesting
those environments are finding it so
painful to request them that they are
keeping them as long as physically
possible rather than getting new ones.
And that's that that friction moment
where you kind of can identify, okay,
this is a bit of decay from from where
we want to be. Um but the opportunity
costs is as well. So, can you identify
that we didn't pick up that feature we
wanted to put into the product because
we didn't have time because it would
have taken us 2 weeks to be able to get
all the infrastructure in place and and
the testing done and all these things
because we didn't have access to what we
needed from the platform. So, those are
two areas where I try and look for for
measurements if we can get it.
>> Right. Yes. Yeah, I think I mean I I've
made this advice I I've I've given this
advice out so many times,
but I also think one of the things here
is is
you have to be able to go back and
explain to a business stakeholder using
business language why something is worth
doing.
Um and if you can't do that, well, it
probably isn't worth the business
funding your stairs. Do you know what I

to check it back to
I don't know. If we pay down this bit of
technical debt, then this behavior that
we're seeing will stop happening and
this is why that matters rather than
just, you know, well, I quite fancy
fixing this thing cuz it annoys me.
Um it's it's a lot of it is just about
framing and understanding where the
where how the business is viewing your
work is is really helpful and having
some sort of It's not quite ubiquitous
language, but having some sort of common
language and common framing that you can
use is really helpful as well, I think.
>> And I I do find with platform
engineering in particular, people often
want to talk about developer experience,
which I'm a huge advocate for experience
of a product. So, I think it's important
we talk about it. But, often developer
experience falls below the must-have
funding line for an organization quite
quickly if they end up needing to to
pivot or change up funding or you know,
something else comes up. So, I think
pinning a whole platform to developer
experience is
uh is maybe not the best pinning for the
the whole platform, right? It can be a
part of the outcomes, but maybe not the
whole because
um
what is it that the platform's meaning
to deliver? It's probably trying to
deliver cost savings or it's trying to
deliver security improvements or it's
trying to deliver speed improvements.
Those are Those are the three most
common cases: faster, safer, more
efficient. Um
>> Right.
>> And
uh developer experience is key to
adoption, so it needs to be something
you think about if you're delivering the
platform, but making the case for the
platform is going to fall under probably
one of those faster, safer, more
efficient categories first and foremost.
And uh I think
yeah, that that's what I've noticed. I
mean, I I've managed to push through a
change from a 2-week delivery cycle uh
delivery train um
into continuous delivery
you know, multiple deployments a day
as a as a major project we worked on as
an organization because I didn't talk
about Kubernetes, I didn't talk about uh
GitLab that we were using at the time. I
didn't talk about any of the tech. I
took a calendar and said, "Do you know
how many times engineers need to touch
this thing in a month?" And I put colors
on the calendar. Said, "Do you know how
many times that we have incidents with
our customers?" I put another color on
the calendar. And I put that calendar in
front of the leadership team and said,
"We can change this calendar to make it
look like this if you'd like. This is
the the kind of cost to get there." And
um my conversations with the engineers
who were coming on board looked a very
different. Uh but the the conversations
for why are we doing this work and
getting the budget
were in business language. So, I think
that's what we're just all trying to do
to the best of our abilities. So.
>> Yes, absolutely. Absolutely.
So, we started I started in the intro by
sort of framing this conversation around
AI. So, I think we should probably shift
and and talk a bit about AI.
Um and obviously coding assistants, you
know, Claude AI and GitHub Copilot and
so forth have been very widely adopted
at this point. But most of the
productivity gains that I'm seeing
people talk about anyway seem to stay at
the individual developer level.
So, from a from a platform engineering
perspective, what's the AI opportunity,
would you say?
>> I think in across the whole industry
we're seeing opportunity everywhere,
aren't we? I think
I have been classifying the AI
opportunity in a few different angles on
platforms. So, first of all, you've got
the AI opportunity just like software
engineers do to build platforms faster
by leveraging coding agents to build
those those platform features. Now, to
be clear, I'm I'm talking here about
using agents to build deterministic
code. So, it's not about, you know, just
throw your AI agent behind all requests
to your platform and and let it go wild.
We'll talk about, you know, my beliefs
in that in a minute, but this is, you
know, using agents to to create your

But, where I think the highest leverage
bit is is still that in the individual
engineer
category, possibly, but is that that
individual engineer can trust its agents

the platform APIs, which means that
they're going to stay on the rails of
the organization.
So,
we talk about like in XP and extreme

more of it.
Uh
AI is is doing that whether or not
you're ready.
So,
um you know, getting getting
capabilities that are business compliant
uh from your platform might be painful
in your organization today, and AI is
sure as heck turning up the dial on how
much we're doing that, and it's putting
the pressure on making that a better
process. So, we're seeing a lot of AI
pressure on consumption of the platform
um as as well as the producing of it.
So,
>> So, that's really interesting. So,
you're you're basically saying that the
AI is the consumer of the platform
rather than the executor of
capabilities.

deterministic if I'm understanding Have

holistically,
the platform is where the rubber hits

there are kind of real-world
implications about how you are going to

non-deterministic
hands? I don't know. Now, there are

deterministic
confidence in their infrastructure layer

the value of agentic AI at the more

end users. So.

there's almost like sort of multiple
levels of this. So, you have as I say,
individual developers using, you know,
code guide or something like code guide

that um
this is again where we're trying I think
to
to we we need to try and apply hard

to these new

an agent or the request for an outcome

that have a lot of business logic in
